claims.text: Differential atomic mobility during heating causes local elemental segregation at the surface of Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles.
Surface segregation creates a disordered, liquid-like premelting layer.
The liquid-like surface layer forms well below the overall bulk melting point.
Differences among the constituent elements' diffusion coefficients govern the staggered melting behavior.
Differences among the constituent elements' melting temperatures govern the staggered melting behavior.
High configurational entropy accentuates the effects of elemental diffusion and melting-temperature differences.
Elements having lower melting points and/or higher diffusion coefficients preferentially migrate toward the nanoparticle surface during heating.
During premelting, the surface is liquid-like while the nanoparticle core remains solid.
Chemical complexity and diffusion differences delay complete homogenization during cooling.
Controlled cooling affects the formation or consolidation of a single-phase high-entropy-alloy solid solution.
Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles will begin surface premelting earlier than monometallic or bimetallic nanoparticles under analogous conditions.
Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles will exhibit a broader melting transition than monometallic or bimetallic nanoparticles.
Greater differences in elemental diffusion behavior will produce a thicker or more extensive premelted layer.
Slower cooling rates will produce greater premelting by allowing enhanced surface mobility.
Monometallic and binary nanoparticles typically melt more uniformly and abruptly, without significant premelting surface segregation.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply primarily to nanoparticles smaller than approximately 100 nm because of their significant surface-to-volume ratios and appreciable atomic mobility.
The relevant premelting window is approximately 70–90% of the bulk melting temperature.
Rapid quenching can suppress the surface diffusion required by the proposed mechanism.
Strain, particle morphology, and minor impurities may also influence the thermal response.
Failure to detect both surface elemental segregation and a liquid-like surface layer during otherwise uniform melting would falsify the proposed segregation-governed premelting mechanism.
